Parsing
• Implementation of parsers
• Two approaches
– Top-down
– Bottom-up
• First: Top-Down
– Easier to understand and program manually
• Then: Bottom-Up
– More powerful and used by most parser generators 
1

Top down Parsing
• Top-down parsing is a parsing technique in which we start constructing the parse tree from the root 
node and move towards the leaf nodes. 
• The root represents the start symbol of the grammar. 
• At every step, we select a production rule to expand a non-terminal into terminals and/or other non-
terminals. 
• The parser continues expanding nodes until the generated symbols match the input string. 
• Therefore, the direction of construction is from top to bottom. 
• The nodes of the parse tree are created in preorder—the parent node is processed before its children. 
• Another important way to understand top-down parsing is through derivation. 
• Top-down parsing attempts to find a leftmost derivation of the given input string. 
• In leftmost derivation, the leftmost non-terminal is expanded first at every step. 
• Common top-down parsing techniques include recursive descent parsing and predictive (LL) parsing
2

Example … Parse Tree Construction Steps
1. Start with the root node
• The root is labelled with the start symbol of the grammar (Ex: <S> or <program> or <type>).
2. Repeat two steps until the tree is complete
•
Step 1: Expansion (Which production?)
•
If the current node is a non-terminal (like <expr> or <stmt>), we must choose one of its 
grammar rules (productions).
•
Example: If <expr> → <expr> + <term> | <term>, we must decide which production rule applies.
•
After choosing, expand it by creating child nodes for each symbol in the production.
•
Step 2: Next node (Which node?)
•
After expanding, we look for the next non-terminal node in the tree that still needs to be 
expanded.
•
This continues until all non-terminals are replaced with terminal symbols (tokens from the input 
program).
Decides how to expand a non-terminal.
Decides where to expand next in the tree.

Back-tracking is not desirable therefore, take help of a “look ahead” token here (array).

Recursive Descent Parsing → Notes
• Easy to implement by hand
• Somewhat inefficient (due to backtracking)
• But does not always work … 
When Recursive Descent Does Not Work 
This is left-recursive because the non-terminal S 
appears at the leftmost position on the right-hand 
side of its own production.
            S⇒Sa⇒Saa⇒Saaa⇒⋯
11

Why Recursive Descent Fails
• Recursive descent works when the grammar is predictive (LL(1)):
• No left recursion
• No ambiguity
• Parser can decide the production by looking at the next input token (1 lookahead)
Fixing the Grammar (Remove Left Recursion)
12
•
Consider the left-recursive production:  S → Sa | ε. 
•
This causes recursive descent to repeatedly call S() without consuming any input, resulting in infinite recursion. 
Therefore, we need to eliminate left recursion before using recursive descent. 
•
Introduce a new non-terminal S′ and transform the grammar into: 
•
S → ε S′ 
•
S′ → a S′ | ε 
•
Since εS′ is equivalent to S′, this can also be written as: S → S′ and S′ → aS′ | ε. 
•
The new grammar is right-recursive, so the parser can consume a tokens before making further recursive calls. 
•
Therefore, left-recursion elimination makes the grammar suitable for recursive descent/predictive parsing.

Left Factoring
• In top-down parsing when it is not clear which production to choose for expansion of a symbol.
•
In general, if A → αβ1 | αβ2 
•
Notice that both alternatives begin with the same common prefix α. 
•
When the parser sees α, it cannot yet determine whether to choose αβ₁ or αβ₂. 
•
Therefore, we defer the decision until enough input has been seen.
Therefore A → αβ1 | αβ2 
→→ transforms to →→
A →αA’
A’ →β1 | β2
Here:
•
 α = the common prefix
•
A′ = a new non-terminal that handles the “rest of the options.”

Summary of Recursive Descent
• Simple and general parsing strategy Left-recursion must be eliminated first … but 
that can be done automatically 
• Unpopular because of backtracking 
• Thought to be too inefficient 
• In practice, backtracking is eliminated by restricting the grammar
25

Predictive Parsers 
• Like recursive-descent but parser can “predict” which production to use
 
– By looking at the next few tokens
 
– No backtracking
• Predictive parsers designed for LL(k) grammars
 
– L means “left-to-right” scan of input
 
– L means “leftmost derivation”
 
– k means “predict based on k tokens of lookahead”
• In practice, LL(1) is used 
• For example, LL(1) uses only one next input token to decide which production to apply.
26

Predictive parsing Contd.,
• Predictive parser can be implemented by maintaining an external stack
27
If M [X, a] contains a production such as X → α, the 
parser removes X from the stack and pushes the symbols 
of α onto the stack.

Parsing algorithm
• The parser considers 'X' the symbol on top of stack, and 'a' the current input symbol 
• These two symbols determine the action to be taken by the parser 
• Assume that '$' is a special token that is at the bottom of the stack and terminates the input 
string.
28
Both stack and input have reached end marker. parser halts, meaning parsing is 
successful.
Stack symbol matches the current input token. Parser pops X 
from the stack and advances the input pointer to the next token.
If M[X,a] contains no valid production, the parser 
reports a syntax error.
Algorithm repeatedly checks, matches, expands, or reports an error until the entire input is successfully parsed.

LL(1) Languages 
• In recursive-descent, for each non-terminal and input token there may be a 
choice of production
• LL(1) means that for each non-terminal and token there is only one production
• Can be specified via 2D tables
 
– One dimension for current non-terminal to expand
 
– One dimension for next token
 
– A table entry contains one production

32

Constructing Parse Table
• Table can be constructed if for every non terminal, every lookahead symbol can be handled by at 
most one production 
 
 
One table cell → at most one production.
• FIRST(α) is the set of terminals that can appear as the first token of strings derived from α.
• For example: A → aB | cD | ε  → → Then: FIRST(A) = { a, c, ε }
• FOLLOW(X) is the set of terminals that can appear immediately after X in some sentential form.
• For example: S → aXb, Here: b ∈ FOLLOW(X), because b can occur immediately after X.
34

First
• The FIRST set of a grammar symbol (terminal or non-terminal) is the set of terminals that can appear at the 
beginning of strings derived from that symbol.
Rules to Compute FIRST:
1. If X is a terminal →         FIRST(X) = { X }
2. If X → ε (X can produce epsilon) →       ε ∈ FIRST(X)
3. If X is a non-terminal and has production: X → Y1 Y2 Y3 … Yn
Then:
•
Add FIRST(Y1) to FIRST(X) (excluding ε).
•
If Y1 ⇒* ε, then also add FIRST(Y2), and so on.
•
If all Y1, Y2, … Yn can derive ε, then add ε to FIRST(X).
FIRST helps in predictive parsing to decide which production to use.
35

Follow
• The FOLLOW set of a non-terminal A is the set of terminals that can appear immediately to the 
right of A in some derivation
Rules to Compute FOLLOW:
1. For the start symbol S:            $ ∈ FOLLOW(S) (end of input marker).
2. If there is a production A → αBβ:
•
Add FIRST(β)    (excluding ε)  to FOLLOW(B).
3. If there is a production A → αB or A → αBβ where β ⇒* ε:
•
Add FOLLOW(A) to FOLLOW(B).
FOLLOW helps in cases when ε is in FIRST, to know where parsing can continue.
37
